headline: New moon springs set up the first real PM flood window at Kings Point since June
subhead: After a week of warm, sloppy bay water pushing fluke out of the back bays, the Sound's tide clock is finally lining up sunset with the flood — and that's when the bass show.
body_markdown:
Last week was one of those stretches where the water looked good but the timing was off. We had warm surface temps building in the back bays — Little Neck, Manhasset, Hempstead Harbor all running warm and a little greasy on calm afternoons — and that warmth did what it always does: it pushed the fluke out of the shallow bay water and down into the channels and toward the inlets, chasing cooler, cleaner water and the bait that goes with it. I saw the same pattern play out on the South Shore with Great South Bay running near 79 degrees, and our Western Sound bays aren't far behind it. The bass, meanwhile, were around — Execution Rocks and the Stepping Stones rockpile never fully shut off — but the good tide stages kept falling in the middle of the day, which on the Sound in July means bright sun, slack current, and fish sitting deep and sour instead of up and hunting.

This week the calendar does us a favor. We're building toward a new moon, which means spring tides are stacking up fast, and more importantly, the timing of the flood at Kings Point is sliding into the sunset hours starting Friday. That's the window I've been waiting on since the June full moon — high stand converging with last light, peaking Saturday through Monday, July 11th through 13th. When that happens on the Western Sound, the bait gets pushed hard up against structure right as the light drops and the bass turn predator instead of just holding station. If you've fished Execution Rocks or the Stepping Stones light long enough, you know this rhythm — the fish don't really turn on until the moon and the tide agree with each other, and for the first time in weeks, they will.

As for what's actually coming over the rail — it's a mixed bag right now, and I'll be straight with you. Striped bass have been present but scattered, mostly schoolie-to-mid-twenties class fish, with the better ones showing on the last two hours of the outgoing off Execution Rocks in 25 to 35 feet, working bucktails — the white 1-ounce with a chunk of pork rind or a 4-inch white Bass Assassin trailer — bounced slow along the rock edges where the current breaks. A few boats working live bunker on a three-way rig off Matinecock Point have connected with better fish, 28 to 34 inches, but you need to find the pods first, and the bunker have been thinner and more scattered than a typical early July push. When you find them stacked, though, that's your green light — snap on a weighted treble, snag one, and free-line it back into the school on 20-pound fluoro leader.

Bluefish have filled in some of the gaps. Choppers in the 3 to 6 pound range are chewing through diamond jigs and Kastmasters off Hart Island and along the Throgs Neck rip on the last of the incoming, especially in that hour around the tide change when the current slows enough for the blues to stack up and feed instead of get pushed through. Wire leader is not optional right now — I lost two bucktails to blues Tuesday because I got lazy and fished straight fluoro.

Fluke inside the Sound have followed the same logic as everywhere else this summer — warm shallow water, cooler deep water, fish moving to find the difference. Your best drifts have been in the deeper channel edges near Throgs Neck Bridge and the drop-off on the Stepping Stones side, 30 to 40 feet, dragging 4-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, slow and tight to bottom on the outgoing. Nothing spectacular — a fish or two in the 3 to 5 pound range per trip if you put your time in and keep moving — but it's honest fishing, not a pile-up.

Porgies remain the one thing you can count on. Execution Rocks and the rockpiles off Matinecock are stacked with them in 20 to 30 feet, and small hooks with clam or squid strips on a high-low rig will fill a bucket without much drama. If you want a guaranteed bend in the rod for the kids, that's still your play.

I'll be straight about weakfish too — it's been quiet, and I mean quiet. The water's warm enough on paper, but paper doesn't catch fish, and I haven't heard of a single decent weakfish report out of our zone or anywhere close to it. I'm not chasing that one right now, and I wouldn't recommend you do either.

Looking ahead: if the wind lays down Friday and Saturday night like the pattern suggests, I'd be fishing the last two hours of daylight into dark at the Stepping Stones light and off Execution Rocks, right on that flood tide convergence. That's the best setup I've seen in weeks — new moon springs, sunset timing, and bait that's been building all month around Matinecock. It's not a guaranteed pile of stripers, but the ingredients are all there for the first time since June, and that's exactly the kind of alignment that's put fish in my boat for thirty years. Plan B if the bass don't cooperate — work the fluke drift off Throgs Neck on the outgoing and fill in with porgies at the rockpiles. Something's going to eat this weekend. The question is just how big.
